newsitem.title: UK: West pushes Bosnia towards economic independence.
newsitem.headline: West pushes Bosnia towards economic independence.

text.p: The international community on Thursday pressed Bosnia to take concrete steps towards economic independence and eventually end its reliance on international aid.

The European Union and the World Bank, two of the main aid donors to Bosnia, told delegates at a high-level conference reviewing the first year of peace in the former Yugoslav republic that the international community remained ready to help but economic reform would be vital.

"During the (peace) consolidation period, emphasis should gradually be shifted from aid for reconstruction to support for economic reforms in order to support self-sustaining growth," the two bodies said in a joint statement.

European Commissioner for External Affairs, Hans van den Broek, said the EU would urge Bosnia to set up its own economic institutions and prepare them to take responsibility from the international community.

"The Commission intends to concentrate in particular on...helping to restructure the economy and put market economy structures in place. This includes setting up a banking system, customs service etc," he said.
"In its programmes over time (the emphasis) will move from aid for reconstruction to support for appropriate economic policies and reform."

No one at the conference is underestimating the enormity of the reconstruction task, with the World Bank reckoning $5.1 billion will be required in total to stabilise the country by the end of the century.

But rebuilding work in the shattered Balkan state is likely to remain patchy as long as parties in Bosnia drag their feet on full compliance with the terms of the Dayton accord which brought peace to the region after 43 months of war.
Bosnia's Serb entity, the Republika Srpska, has been criticised for failing to hand over indicted war criminals and allow the return of refugees.
It has therefore received only two percent of the reconstruction cash paid out to Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation, and the World Bank said this would have to change.
"It will be necessary to increase the proportion of aid to the Republika Srpska in the consolidation period so as to meet the aim of distribution according to needs," it said.
The EU and the World Bank said a second pledging conference was due to be held late in February 1997.
"A primary goal for 1997 will be to obtain pledges of $1.4 billion to finance the reconstruction needs of the first year of the consolidation plan," they said.

But van den Broek conceded it was difficult for donor governments to go to their tax payers and ask them to spend billions if no efforts were being made by the Bosnians themselves to meet the conditionality terms.
Of some $1.8 billion pledged at a Brussels conference in April, the World Bank said $700 million had already been disbursed.

But it stressed that Bosnian politics had hampered particular projects, especially in the telecommunications sector, while compliance with the terms of peace would determine the West's willingness to continue to help.
"The willingness of the international community to provide support on this scale will depend on the parties' compliance with the peace agreement and economic policy commitments," it said.
